13. Mr Khan then turns his attention on the merit of the appeal and submits that the trial Court on consideration of the pleadings, the evidence adduced by the parties and taking into consideration the materials on record rightly found that the plaintiffs have complied with the formalities of Talab-i-Muw-sibat and Talab-i-Ishhad within the meaning of the Muslim Law. in elaborating his argument on this point, he submits that the plaintiff No. 2 has performed those formalities for and on behalf of plaintiff No. 1 and on his behalf though at the time of deposition he stated that he made the Talabs for pre-empting the properties under the Muslim Law and there is no discrepancy in the evidence of PWs. The learned Advocate for the respondent submits that there is no specific form for performing the Talab-i-Muwsibat though certain formalities have been laid down for the performance of Talab-i-Ishhad and from the deposition of PW 1 it becomes clear that the specific intention for pre-empting the suit land by the plaintiffs have been expressed on 9--1997 by performing the Talab-i-Muwsibat on the suit land. Mr Khan further submitted that it does not lie in the mouth of the appellant to say that the plaintiffs have failed to prove their ownership in the 'B' Schedule land, inasmuch as the DWs in one voice admitted in their evidence that to the contiguous south of the suit land, the land of the plaintiffs are situated. Mr Khan submitted that there is sufficient oral evidence adduced by the plaintiffs stating that they are the purchaser of 'B' Schedule land and the certified copies of the deeds in question have been exhibited by the plaintiffs before the trial Court and the original title deeds could not be produced as they are lying with the Bank. In elaborating his submission he further submits that besides the PWs the DWs also admitted that the plaintiffs are the owner of the 'B' Schedule land and the legal position is that things admitted need not be proved. There-fore, even in the absence of any evidence the trial Court is justified in arriving at a finding that the plaintiffs are the real owner of the 'B' Schedule land and thereby the first pre-requisite for filing of the suit for pre-emption by the plaintiffs have been fulfilled. Mr Khan further submitted that Mr Tabarak Hussain forcefully argued that the suit lands are not agricultural land and are commercial plots, but this submission is contrary to material and evidence on record. Exhibits 5(Kha) and 3 (Gha) i.e. Khatian and rent receipt, as well as the title deeds of the defendant No. 1 show that the suit land is agricultural land and the 'B' Schedule land is Chala land and Chala land is also agricultural land within the meaning of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951. Therefore, it cannot be said that the lands in question are commercial plots and therefore, cannot be a subject matter of pre-emption under the Muslim Law. Mr Khan further submitted that to prove the ownership of the 'B' Schedule land the plaintiffs produced and exhibited current rent receipts which have been admitted without any objection and it is now well settled that khatian and rent receipts are documents of possession and collateral documents of title as has been laid down in 35 DLR (AD) 216. Mr Khan further submitted that it has been contended by the appellants that the plaintiffs did not make the Talab-i-Ishhad promptly but there is no basis for that as admitted facts show that the plaintiffs first came to know about the sale in question on 9-3-1997 and on the next date sent their man to the local Registry Office and obtained the certified copy of the sale deeds on 18-3-1997 when the plaintiffs acquired a definite know-ledge as to the sale of the suit lands by the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 to the defendant No. 1 and then on 19-3-1997 made Talab-i-Ishhad. Mr Enayet Hossain Khan in the course of argument also submitted that in a suit for pre-emption the plaintiffs need not establish their title, inasmuch as the title of the plaintiffs is not in issue and it has been categorically stated by the plaintiffs in their plaint that they are owner by purchase of the 'B' Schedule land which has not been denied by the defendants in their written statement. Therefore, it must be presumed that the defendants have admitted the aforesaid statement of the plaintiffs and now they cannot resale from that and take a different stand giving a go-by to the earlier stand. Mr Khan also submitted that the trial Court has rightly taken the view that the boundary wall erected in between the 'A' and 'B' Schedule lands cannot stand in the way of the plaintiffs to get an order of pre-emption in their favour inasmuch as the 'B' Schedule land is contiguous to 'A' Schedule land. 

 29. Let us, now, discuss about the merits of the appeals. The defendants have denied the ownership of the plaintiffs in the "B" Schedule land in paragraph No. 12 of the written statement as well as DW 1 has denied it in his evidence. As against that the plaintiffs made out a case in their plaint that they are the owners by purchase of the "B" Schedule land but at the time of adducing evidence except the word of PW 1 there is no other documentary evidence to show that they are the real owners of the "B" Schedule land. It is stated by PW 1 that the original title deeds are lying with the bank and a letter to that effect of the Bank was produced but they have not admitted in evidence the certified copy of the title deeds. Mr Tabarak Hussain empathically argued on this point submitting that it is pre-requisite for the plaintiffs to prove their ownership in the contiguous land. Even before this Court the plaintiff respondent did not file any application under Order XL, rule 31 of the Code to admit those documents as additional evidence. Moreover, there is no explanation why they have not exhibited the title deeds which are the most important documents for proving the title of the plaintiffs to 'B' Schedule land. To counter the arguments of Mr Hussain, Mr Khan appearing for the plaintiff-respondent tried to impress upon us that though title deeds have not been exhibited nevertheless khatians and rent receipts which are collateral documents of title have been produced and exhibited. Mr Khan relying on the decision reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216 submitted that record of rights and rent receipts are collateral documents of title and these are sufficient to establish the title of the plaintiff. As against that, Mr Hussain has submitted that in a pre-emption suit it is the sine qua non to establish the ownership of the plaintiff and by withholding the original documents without giving any explanation and production of Khatian and rent receipts are not sufficient to establish the title and in support of his contention he has relied on the decision reported in 12 DLR 93. In this connection it may further be mentioned that though they have produced some certified copies of the deeds but that only relates to 2.58 acres of land and regarding the rest of the land no title deed has been filed and ignoring this material aspect of the case, the trial Court arrived at a finding that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their owner-ship simply on the ground that even the DWs have admitted plaintiffs' ownership. This observation of the trial Court appears to be based on misreading of the evidence of DWs. It appears that DW 1 categorically denied the ownership of the plaintiffs and the other DWs admitted that the plaintiffs are in possession of the 'B' Schedule land. But they did not indicate the nature of possession as to whether they possess it as owners or otherwise. It is now well established that in a pre-emption suit the plaintiff must establish his exclusive ownership into the contiguous land as Shafi-i-Jar. Therefore, finding of the trial Court that the plaintiffs are the owners of the 'B' Schedule land is erroneous and against weight of evidence.
